config.title: WebSockets with Express

intro.title: WebSockets with Express
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build a real-time chat application using WebSockets with Express. You will learn how to establish a persistent, two-way communication channel between a client and server, enabling instant message updates without page reloads. The core programming concept involves handling WebSocket connections, events, and broadcasting messages to multiple clients. You will use the Express framework to set up the server and the 'ws' library to implement WebSocket functionality. This hands-on project will help you understand how real-time features work in modern web applications.
intro.usecase: WebSockets enable real-time, bidirectional communication between clients and servers, making them essential for interactive applications. In real-world software, you'll see WebSockets powering live chat applications like Slack or Discord, where messages appear instantly without page refreshes. They're also crucial for collaborative tools like Google Docs, where multiple users can edit simultaneously and see each other's changes in real-time. Additionally, WebSockets drive live dashboards for stock trading platforms, sports score trackers, and IoT device monitoring systems that require constant data updates. As a developer, implementing WebSockets in Express allows you to build responsive, engaging applications that feel immediate and interactive to users.

objectives: Configure an Express server to support WebSocket connections
Initialize a WebSocket server instance within an Express application
Implement WebSocket event handlers for client connections and messages
Manipulate WebSocket connections to broadcast messages to multiple clients
Integrate WebSocket functionality with existing Express routes and middleware
Construct a basic real-time chat application using WebSockets and Express
Control WebSocket connection lifecycle including opening, closing, and error handling

steps.title: Import Express and WebSocket dependencies
steps.instruction: Import Express, the createServer function from the http module, and the WebSocket.Server class from the ws package.
steps.hint: Use require() statements to import the necessary modules. Remember that ws is typically installed as a separate package.
steps.seedCode: // Import Express, createServer from http, and WebSocket.Server from ws
steps.expectedOutcome: The server file will have the required imports set up for building a WebSocket-enabled Express application.
successCriteria: Express, http.createServer, and ws.WebSocket.Server are imported using require() statements.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but check that you've imported all three required items: Express, createServer from http, and WebSocket.Server from ws.
steps.feedbackWrong: The imports are not complete. Make sure to import Express, the createServer function from http, and the WebSocket.Server class from ws.

steps.title: Initialize Express app and HTTP server
steps.instruction: Create an Express app instance and an HTTP server using the imported createServer function.
steps.hint: Call express() to create the app, then pass the app to createServer() to create the server.
steps.seedCode:
// Import Express, createServer from http, and WebSocket.Server from ws

// Create Express app instance and HTTP server
steps.expectedOutcome: You'll have an Express app instance and an HTTP server ready for WebSocket integration.
successCriteria: An Express app instance is created with express() and an HTTP server is created with createServer(app).
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you're creating both the Express app instance and the HTTP server.
steps.feedbackWrong: This step requires creating both an Express app instance and an HTTP server. Check the imports and function calls.

steps.title: Create WebSocket server instance
steps.instruction: Initialize a WebSocket server instance and attach it to your HTTP server.
steps.hint: Use the WebSocket.Server constructor with the server option set to your HTTP server variable.
steps.analogousExample:
// Create WebSocket server attached to HTTP server
const wss = new WebSocket.Server({ server: httpServer });
steps.expectedOutcome: A WebSocket server instance is created and attached to your HTTP server, ready to handle WebSocket connections.
successCriteria: WebSocket server instance is created with the correct constructor and attached to the HTTP server.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close! Make sure you're using the WebSocket.Server constructor with the server option set to your HTTP server.
steps.feedbackWrong: The WebSocket server wasn't properly initialized. Check that you're using the correct constructor and attaching it to the HTTP server.

steps.title: Set up WebSocket connection event handler
steps.instruction: Add a 'connection' event listener to your WebSocket server instance to handle new client connections.
steps.hint: Use the wsServer.on('connection', ...) method to listen for connection events.
steps.expectedOutcome: The WebSocket server will now be able to detect when new clients connect.
successCriteria: A 'connection' event listener is added to wsServer with a callback function.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're adding the event listener to the wsServer instance and using the correct event name 'connection'.
steps.feedbackWrong: The connection event handler wasn't properly set up. Check that you're calling wsServer.on('connection', ...) with a callback function.

steps.title: Handle incoming WebSocket messages
steps.instruction: Inside the WebSocket connection event handler, add a 'message' event listener to the individual connection object (ws) that logs received messages to the console.
steps.hint: Use ws.on('message', callback) where the callback receives the incoming data. The data can be logged with console.log().
steps.expectedOutcome: The WebSocket server will now log any messages sent from connected clients to the console.
successCriteria: A 'message' event listener is added to the ws parameter inside the connection handler, and it logs the received data.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you're adding the event listener to the ws parameter (the individual connection) and logging the data.
steps.feedbackWrong: The message handler is missing or incorrect. Remember to use ws.on('message', callback) inside the connection handler.

steps.title: Broadcast messages to all connected clients
steps.instruction: Inside the WebSocket connection handler, create a function named 'broadcast' that takes a 'message' parameter and sends it to all connected clients using wsServer.clients.forEach().
steps.hint: The broadcast function should iterate through wsServer.clients and call ws.send(message) for each client connection.
steps.expectedOutcome: A broadcast function is defined inside the connection handler that can send messages to all connected WebSocket clients.
successCriteria: The broadcast function is created with a 'message' parameter and uses wsServer.clients.forEach() to send the message to each client.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure your broadcast function takes a 'message' parameter and uses wsServer.clients.forEach() to send it to each client.
steps.feedbackWrong: The broadcast function isn't quite right. It should be defined inside the connection handler, take a 'message' parameter, and use wsServer.clients.forEach() to send the message to all connected clients.

steps.title: Set up Express static file serving
steps.instruction: Configure Express to serve static files from a directory named 'public' using the built-in express.static middleware.
steps.hint: Use app.use() with express.static() and pass the directory name as a string.
steps.analogousExample:
// Serving static files from a 'public' directory
app.use(express.static('public'));
steps.expectedOutcome: The Express app will serve HTML, CSS, and JavaScript files from a 'public' directory, allowing you to create a client-side WebSocket testing interface.
successCriteria: Express is configured to serve static files from a 'public' directory using app.use(express.static('public')).
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're using express.static() with the directory name 'public' and app.use() to apply it.
steps.feedbackWrong: configure Express to serve static files from a directory called 'public' using the built-in middleware.

steps.title: Create basic HTML client interface
steps.instruction: Create a new file named 'index.html' in your project directory with a basic HTML structure that includes an input field and a button for sending WebSocket messages.
steps.hint: You can create a simple HTML file with <input> and <button> elements inside a <form> or <div>. The input should have an id attribute for JavaScript to reference later.
steps.expectedOutcome: You should have an index.html file with input and button elements ready for WebSocket client functionality.
successCriteria: An index.html file exists with an input field and a button element for sending messages.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've created an HTML file, but make sure it includes both an input field and a button element for sending messages.
steps.feedbackWrong: The HTML file is missing or doesn't include the required input and button elements for WebSocket messaging.

steps.title: Add WebSocket client-side JavaScript
steps.instruction: Create a new file named 'client.js' in your project directory and add JavaScript code to connect to the WebSocket server, handle sending messages from a form, and display received messages.
steps.hint: Create a new file in the same directory as your server.js file. Use the WebSocket API to connect to 'ws://localhost:8080' and add event listeners for 'open', 'message', and 'close' events.
steps.expectedOutcome: A new client.js file is created with WebSocket connection code that can connect to the server, send messages, and handle incoming messages.
successCriteria: The client.js file exists and contains WebSocket connection code with event handlers for connection, message reception, and message sending functionality.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've started the client.js file, but it's missing some WebSocket functionality. Make sure to include all the event handlers needed for a complete WebSocket client.
steps.feedbackWrong: The client.js file doesn't contain the expected WebSocket client code. Review the WebSocket API documentation and ensure you're creating a proper WebSocket connection with event handlers.

steps.title: Start the server and test WebSocket functionality
steps.instruction: Start the HTTP server by calling server.listen() on port 3000 and add a console log to confirm it's running.
steps.hint: Use server.listen(3000, () => { console.log(...) }) to start the server and log a message.
steps.expectedOutcome: The server will start and log a message to the console, making the WebSocket application accessible for testing in a browser.
successCriteria: The server is started on port 3000 with a console log message confirming it's running.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've added some server startup code, but make sure to include both the port (3000) and a console log message.
steps.feedbackWrong: The server startup code is missing or incorrect. You need to call server.listen() with port 3000 and include a console log.
